title: Learn Anything Fast
description: The meta-skill: how to pick what matters, practise it, and actually remember it. Start here.
keyIdeas: Find the vital few: a small set of concepts usually does most of the work.
Test yourself instead of rereading — **retrieval** is what builds memory.
Space your reviews out, and review right before you'd forget.
Mix problem types so you learn *when* to use each idea.
Explain it simply. Where you get stuck is what you don't understand yet.

concepts.label: 80/20 rule
concepts.summary: A small share of causes produces most of the results, so effort is not equally valuable everywhere.

concepts.label: Core of a subject
concepts.summary: The few ideas that appear constantly and that many others depend on, filtered by your goal; learn them first and deeply.

concepts.label: Long tail
concepts.summary: The many rarely used details: postpone them until your goal needs them, which means "not yet", not "never".

concepts.label: Active recall
concepts.summary: Pulling an answer out of memory before looking, which strengthens memory more than restudying (the testing effect).

concepts.label: Illusion of competence
concepts.summary: Material that looks familiar feels learned, but recognizing an answer is much easier than producing it.

concepts.label: Effortful learning
concepts.summary: Practice that feels harder (retrieving, spacing, mixing) builds more durable memory, and mistakes with feedback are learning moments.

concepts.label: Forgetting curve
concepts.summary: Without review memory fades fast and then more slowly; each successful recall flattens the curve.

concepts.label: Spaced repetition
concepts.summary: Spreading reviews over growing gaps, each timed for just before you would forget, beats cramming the same total time.

concepts.label: Leitner box
concepts.summary: A card moves up a box and waits longer when right, and goes back to box 1 when wrong.

concepts.label: Interleaving
concepts.summary: Mixing problem types (A C B A...) so each problem first makes you choose which method applies.

concepts.label: Blocked practice
concepts.summary: Repeating one problem type until done (AAAA BBBB): smoother, but you never have to pick the method.

concepts.label: Feynman technique
concepts.summary: Explain an idea in plain words; where you hand-wave or reach for jargon is a gap to go back and fill, then simplify.

lessons.title: The 80/20 rule for learning
lessons.takeaway: Learn the high-frequency, load-bearing ideas first; add details only when your goal demands them.

steps.title: The Pareto principle
steps.body:
In many fields, a **small share of causes produces most of the results**. The usual shorthand is *80/20*: roughly 20% of the inputs drive roughly 80% of the outcome.

The exact numbers vary — it might be 90/10 or 70/30 — but the shape is what matters: **effort is not equally valuable everywhere.**

steps.title: Applied to learning
steps.body:
Every subject has a **core**: a handful of ideas that everything else builds on or repeats. Learn the core first and deeply, and the rest becomes easier — often just variations.

- In a language, the most frequent ~1,000 words cover a large majority of everyday text.
- In chess, a few principles (control the center, develop pieces, keep the king safe) guide most opening moves.
- In spreadsheets, a few tools (SUM, IF, lookups, pivot tables) handle most real work.

steps.prompt: You have 10 hours to learn basic statistics for work. What's the most 80/20 plan?
choices: Read the textbook from chapter 1 until time runs out
Identify the few ideas used constantly (averages, spread, sampling, correlation) and practise them on real problems
Watch as many different videos as possible for broad exposure
Memorize every formula in the appendix
steps.hint: Which option spends time in proportion to how often an idea is actually used?
steps.explanation: Spending most of the time on the high-frequency core *and practising it* gives the most usable skill per hour. Reading linearly spends equal time on rarely used material.

steps.title: Finding the core of a topic
steps.problem: How do you find the 20% of a new subject that matters most?
steps: **Look for frequency.** What appears in every exam, every tutorial, every real project? Repeated items are core.
**Look for dependencies.** Which ideas are prerequisites for many others? Those are load-bearing.
**Compare 2–3 syllabi or ask a practitioner.** The overlap between course outlines is a good map of the core.
**Filter by your goal.** 'Read research papers' and 'pass the exam' have different cores.
steps.answer: Core = **high frequency + many dependents**, filtered by *your* goal.

steps.prompt: Which signal best suggests a concept is part of the core?
choices: It appears in the last chapter of the book
It is a prerequisite for many other concepts
It has the most complicated name
It's the newest research result
steps.explanation: Ideas that many others depend on are load-bearing: weak understanding there causes problems everywhere downstream.

steps.prompt: You start an office job next week where you'll build reports from sales data in spreadsheets. Spreadsheets have hundreds of features. Sort what to learn **first** from what can wait.
buckets: Long tail: later, if the job needs it

items.text: SUM and AVERAGE
IF, to handle simple conditions
Lookups (VLOOKUP / XLOOKUP) to pull data from another table
Pivot tables to summarize sales by month or region
Sorting and filtering rows
Writing macros in VBA
Every one of the hundreds of built-in functions
Engineering functions like BESSELJ
The history of spreadsheets since VisiCalc

steps.hint: Use the two signals from the example: does it show up in nearly every report (frequency), and do other skills build on it (dependents)? Then filter by *this* goal.
steps.explanation: **Core:** SUM, IF, lookups, pivot tables and sorting/filtering appear in almost every sales report, and they combine into most of the rest. A week on these gives you most of the day-to-day value. **Long tail:** most functions are rarely used, BESSELJ is for engineers, and the history is interesting but doesn't build reports. Macros are the instructive one: not *never*, just *not yet*. If the job turns out to repeat the same report every Monday, automating it becomes worth learning, and that's the next question's point.

steps.prompt: What's the main *risk* of the 80/20 approach?
choices: It's too slow
Treating 'not yet' as 'never' — the remaining details can matter for your goal
It only works for languages
It requires expensive tools
steps.explanation: 80/20 is about **ordering**: core first, details when your goal needs them. Some goals (surgery, flying a plane) need the long tail too.

lessons.title: Active recall: test, don't reread
lessons.takeaway: Before you look, try to recall. Retrieval builds memory; rereading builds false confidence.

steps.title: Familiar is not the same as remembered
steps.body:
Rereading notes *feels* productive because the material looks familiar. But **familiarity isn't memory** — recognizing an answer is much easier than producing it.

**Active recall** means pulling information out of your head *before* you look: answering questions, writing what you remember, solving a problem without the worked solution. Research on the *testing effect* shows that retrieving information strengthens memory more than restudying it for the same amount of time.

steps.prompt: Which of these are active recall, and which are just passive review? Sort each study habit.
buckets: Passive review: you just see it again

items.text: Closing the book and writing down the main ideas from memory
Answering your flashcards before flipping them
Trying a problem before looking at the worked solution
Explaining the idea out loud without your notes
Taking a practice test
Highlighting the key sentences in a chapter
Rereading your notes twice
Watching the lecture again at 1.5× speed
Copying definitions neatly onto flashcards
Reading the worked solution and nodding along

steps.hint: Ask one question: do you have to *produce* the answer from memory before you see it?
steps.explanation: Only the active ones force **retrieval**: you pull the answer out of your head first, then check. Highlighting, rereading, rewatching and following a worked solution are passive re-exposure; they make the material feel familiar without testing whether you can produce it. Flashcards show the difference best: *copying* definitions onto them is still passive. They only become active recall when you *answer* them before flipping.

steps.title: Struggle is the point
steps.body:
Recall feels harder than rereading, and you'll get things wrong. That's fine — **effortful retrieval** is what makes memories durable, and mistakes followed by feedback are some of the best learning moments.

That's why every lesson here asks you questions instead of only showing you text.

steps.prompt: After studying, Sam feels confident because the notes 'all looked familiar'. What's the best conclusion?
choices: Sam has mastered the material
Familiarity is a weak signal; Sam should test themselves to check
Sam should reread once more to be safe
Sam should switch topics
steps.explanation: Recognition creates an *illusion of competence*. A quick self-test shows what can actually be recalled.

steps.title: Turning notes into questions
steps.problem: Your note says: *'Mitochondria produce ATP through cellular respiration.'* How do you turn it into recall practice?
steps: Rewrite it as a question: **What do mitochondria produce, and through what process?**
Hide the answer and attempt it from memory — out loud or on paper.
Check. If you were wrong, note *why*, and ask the question again later.
steps.answer: Every note becomes a **question you answer before looking**.

steps.prompt: Retrieving information strengthens memory more than restudying it. This finding is called the ___ effect. (one word)
steps.hint: It's what you're doing right now by answering this.

lessons.title: Spaced repetition
lessons.takeaway: Review just before you'd forget, with growing gaps. A few minutes of daily review beats hours of cramming.

steps.title: The forgetting curve
steps.body:
Without review, memory fades quickly at first, then more slowly — the *forgetting curve*, first measured by Hermann Ebbinghaus in the 1880s.

Each successful recall flattens the curve, so you forget more slowly afterwards. That means **the gaps between reviews can grow**: 1 day, then 3, then a week, then a month.

steps.prompt: With the same total study time, which schedule leads to better long-term memory?
choices: 5 hours the night before the exam
Five 1-hour sessions spread over two weeks
steps.explanation: The **spacing effect**: spreading practice over time beats cramming it into one session, especially for long-term retention.

steps.title: When to review
steps.body:
The best moment to review is when you're **about to forget**: hard enough to take effort, easy enough to succeed.

A simple system called the *Leitner box* does this automatically:

- Get a card right → it moves up a box and waits longer.
- Get it wrong → it goes back to box 1 and comes back soon.

The **Review** page in this app works exactly like that.

steps.title: Leitner intervals
steps.problem: In this app the waits are: box 2 → 1 day, box 3 → 3 days, box 4 → 7 days, box 5 → 16 days, box 6 → 35 days. You answer a new question correctly today (day 0). When do you see it again if you keep getting it right?
steps: Correct today → box 2 → next review in **1 day** (day 1).
steps.answer: Four short reviews cover almost a month — far less time than rereading every day.

steps.prompt: Continuing the example: on day 27 you answer correctly again and the card moves to box 6 (35 days). On which day is the next review?
steps.hint: Add the box-6 wait to day 27.
steps.explanation: 27 + 35 = **62**. The gaps keep growing, so each fact costs very little time to maintain.

steps.prompt: You get a box-5 card wrong. What happens in a Leitner system?
choices: It stays in box 5
It moves down to box 4
It goes back to box 1 and comes back soon
It's deleted
steps.explanation: A miss means the memory has faded, so it starts again with short gaps until it's stable.

steps.prompt: A new card's answers go: **right, right, right, right, wrong, right**. Put what this app's Review page does after each answer in order.
items: Wrong → back to box 1, due again right away
Right → wait 1 day: the climb starts over
steps.hint: Each right answer moves the card up one box, and the wait grows. A wrong answer doesn't just step down one box.
steps.explanation: Right answers move the card up a box: 1 day, then 3, then 7, then 16, so the reviews land on days 1, 4, 11 and 27. The miss on day 27 sends it all the way back to **box 1**, due again right away, and the next right answer restarts the climb at **1 day**. Growing gaps for what you know, short gaps for what you've forgotten: that's the spacing effect at work. Every question you answer in this app moves through these same boxes.

lessons.title: Interleaving and the Feynman technique
lessons.takeaway: Mix problem types, and explain ideas simply — where you stumble is exactly what to study next.

steps.title: Interleaving
steps.body:
**Blocked practice:** AAAA BBBB CCCC. **Interleaved practice:** A C B B A C B A…

Blocked practice feels smoother, but in a real test nobody tells you which method to use. Mixing problem types forces you to *choose the right tool*, which is a big part of real skill. Studies in maths and motor learning often find that interleaving improves later test results, even though it feels harder during practice.

steps.prompt: Why do the quizzes in this app mix questions from different lessons?
choices: To make it random for fun
So you practise recognizing *which* idea applies, not just repeating the one you just saw
Because there aren't enough questions
To make quizzes shorter
steps.explanation: Interleaving trains **discrimination**: identifying the type of problem is half the battle.

steps.prompt: Blocked (AAAA BBBB) or interleaved (A C B A…)? Sort each practice session.

items.text: 20 circle-area problems, then 20 triangle-area problems
Tennis: 50 forehands in a row, then 50 backhands
Doing only chapter 5's exercises right after reading chapter 5
Piano: one scale ten times, then the next scale ten times
A worksheet mixing circle, triangle and rectangle problems in random order
Tennis: the coach mixes forehands and backhands without warning
A shuffled flashcard deck covering three topics
This app's quizzes, which mix questions from several lessons

steps.hint: Before each problem, do you already know which method it needs? If yes, it's blocked.
steps.explanation: **Blocked** sessions repeat one type until it's done, so you always know which method comes next. Chapter 5's exercises count too: they all use chapter 5's idea. **Interleaved** sessions mix the types, so each problem first asks *which* method fits, the same question a real test or a real match asks. That choosing is why interleaving often improves later results, even though it tends to feel harder while you practise.

steps.title: The Feynman technique
steps.body:
To check whether you really understand something:

- **Explain it** in plain words, as if to a 12-year-old.
- **Find the gaps.** Where you hand-wave or reach for jargon, you don't understand yet.
- **Go back** to the source to fill exactly those gaps.
- **Simplify** and use an analogy.

It's active recall plus self-diagnosis: it points your effort at your weakest spots.

steps.prompt: While explaining recursion to a friend, you say: *'It just calls itself, you know, the stack handles it.'* What does the Feynman technique tell you?
choices: Great — jargon saves time
That hand-wave marks a gap: go learn exactly how the call stack works during recursion
Switch to an easier topic
Memorize the textbook definition word for word
steps.explanation: Vague phrases and jargon are signs of shallow understanding — and they show you precisely where to study.

steps.prompt: You want to check that you really understand why summer is warmer than winter. Put the Feynman technique's steps in order.
items: Explain it in plain words, as if to a 12-year-old
Notice the shaky part: 'the tilt does… something' is a hand-wave
Go back to a good source and read exactly how the tilt changes the sunlight
Explain it again, simpler, with an analogy: a flashlight shining straight down vs at a slant
steps.hint: You can't find a gap before you try to explain, and you can't fill a gap you haven't found.
steps.explanation: **Explain** first: that's active recall, and it's the only way to find out what you can't say. The hand-wave marks the **gap**. Then go back to the source for *that* gap only, not the whole chapter. (The answer: when your half of the Earth tilts toward the sun, sunlight arrives more directly and days are longer, so each patch of ground gets more energy.) Finally **simplify**: if the flashlight analogy works, you understand it. If you stumble again, loop back.

steps.prompt: Which daily routine uses the most ideas from this topic?
choices: Reread one chapter every morning
10 minutes reviewing due questions + one new core lesson + explaining today's idea in your own words
Watch a 2-hour lecture each weekend
Make beautifully formatted notes
steps.explanation: It combines **spaced repetition** (review), the **80/20 rule** (core lesson), and **active recall + Feynman** (explaining from memory).
